title: Should you ever try again with an ex? Millennial Therapist Dr. Sara Kuburic weighs in - NewsBreak
text:
By Sara Kuburic ,
17 minutes ago Sara Kuburic is an existential psychotherapist, author of the book “It’s On Me” and voice behind the viral Instagram page Millennial Therapist. (Courtesy of Sara Kuburic) Dr. Sara Kuburic is an existential psychotherapist , author of the book “It’s On Me” and voice behind the viral Instagram page Millennial Therapist , which has 1.7M followers. In her debut weekly advice column for CT Insider , she answers questions from a Q&A on her Instagram account.
CT Insider is asking for questions from readers, and Kuburic — who specializes in identity, relationships and trauma, guiding individuals toward lives that feel authentic, free and meaningful — will answer three of them each week. Share yours in the form below and you could see it in a future column.
Should you ever try again with an ex? “They are your ex for a reason” rings true for this question, but probably not for the reasons you think. Most people take this phrase to mean it’s not worth trying again. I interpret it differently: You and your ex broke up for a reason, and you need to make sure the reason is clear if you’re considering round two. For relationship 2.0 to work, you need to know what went wrong the first time around. Trying again and simply hoping for the best is not advice I would give – ever.
Instead, I would suggest exploring and discussing the following:
Do you and your ex agree about what went wrong? What caused the disconnect, transgression, hurt or disinterest in the first place? What needs weren’t met? What role do you each take in the previous relationship ending? Are both of you taking responsibility? How are you going to show up differently this time? Doing the same things and expecting different results doesn’t work, so what’s the new plan? You could consider check-ins, dates, a different relationship structure or personal work, including therapy. Make sure this list is as specific as possible. Instead of saying “we will spend more quality time together,” you can say, “I will put my phone away during dinner” or “we will do a quick check-in at the end of each day.” The desire to make something work is not enough by itself. Actionable steps, communication, and honesty are the best ways to go. Remember, you’re not just building a relationship, you’re re- building one, unlearning lessons and breaking patterns.
Is it OK to feel you should leave someone you love if they can’t meet your needs? The short answer is yes. The Beatles might tell you that all you need is love, but it’s a concept I debunk on an almost daily basis in my clinical practice. Love is necessary, but it’s not enough. We all have needs. Your partner’s ability to fulfil your needs will dictate how content you are in your relationship.
In the same breath, I would also like to mention that I often see individuals place unrealistic expectations on their partners, particularly that they can and should fulfill every need. That is an unfair ask, and it’s the fastest way to set your partner up for failure and yourself for disappointment.
I believe each person has to, first, define which needs they want their partner to meet and, second, acknowledge that some needs have to be outsourced to a friend, mentor or therapist.
What do you do when your partner constantly shuts down and doesn’t share what is upsetting them? This is a really difficult situation. Regardless of whether this is your partner’s way of coping with dysregulation or their lack of communication skills, the outcome is disconnection – and often frustration. Here are some ways of navigating the situation:
If they are unaware of their pattern, lovingly share with them what you have observed. Let them know how their shutting down impacts you and the relationship. Explore how you can co-create an environment in which they will feel more comfortable, safe or willing to share what’s going on for them. Suggest and encourage them to find tools to self-regulate and identify the root cause (e.g., read books, go to therapy, take online courses or journal). Explore what your communication needs are and what will happen if they can’t be met. Is this a dealbreaker for you? Are you OK putting things on pause and addressing them once your partner has had more time to process? Is their lack of communication impacting your connection in a way that makes you want to end the relationship? (I would also like to add that if your partner tries to punish you by withholding communication, this can be a sign of emotional abuse.)
